==Problem==
Emmy says to Max, "I ordered <imath>36</imath> math club sweatshirts today." Max asks, "How much did each shirt cost?" Emmy responds, "I'll give you a hint. The total cost was <imath>\$ \underline A~\underline B~\underline B.\underline B~\underline A</imath>, where <imath>A</imath> and <imath>B</imath> are digits and <imath>A \neq 0</imath>." After a pause, Max says, "That was a good price." What is <imath>A + B</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}~7 \qquad \textbf{(B)}~8 \qquad \textbf{(C)}~11 \qquad \textbf{(D)}~14 \qquad \textbf{(E)}~15</imath>

==Solution 1==
The problem is essentially telling us that <imath>\underline A~\underline B~\underline B.\underline B~\underline A</imath> is divisible by <imath>36</imath>, so it is divisible by <imath>9</imath>. Then, by the divisibility by <imath>9</imath> condition,
<cmath>A+B+B+B+A=2A+3B\equiv 0\pmod{9}</cmath>
This means that <imath>A</imath> must be divisible by <imath>3</imath>, or otherwise <imath>2A+3B</imath> would not be divisible by <imath>3</imath> and thus <imath>9</imath>. Since <imath>A\ne0</imath>, we must have one of <imath>A=3,6,9</imath>.

But <imath>A</imath> must be even or else the entire number would not be even and thus would not be divisible by <imath>4</imath>. Hence <imath>A=6</imath>. Then, <imath>2\cdot 6+3B\equiv 0\pmod{9}</imath>, so <imath>4+B\equiv 0\pmod{3}</imath>, and thus <imath>B\equiv 2\pmod{3}</imath>. This yields <imath>B=2,5,8</imath>, of which <imath>B=5</imath> is the only number that allows <imath>\underline A~\underline B~\underline B.\underline B~\underline A</imath> to be divisible by <imath>4</imath>. Thus the answer is <imath>6+5=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}~11}</imath>.

~ [https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/User:Eevee9406 eevee9406]

==Solution 2 (Trial and Error)==

A number is divisible by <imath>36</imath> if it divisible by <imath>4</imath>, and <imath>9</imath>. The divisibility rule for <imath>4</imath> requires the last 2 digits to also be a multiple of <imath>4</imath>. The divisibility rule for 9 requires the sum of all digits to be divisible by <imath>9</imath>. Using the first condition <imath>A+B</imath> is a multiple of 4. We can list out all possibilities for this, since both <imath>A</imath> and <imath>B</imath> are digits. The possibilities are  <imath>(1,2),(1,6),...(9,6)</imath> for <imath>A</imath>, and <imath>B</imath> respectively. There are a total of <imath>2</imath> digits that are <imath>A</imath>'s and <imath>3</imath> that are <imath>B</imath>'s. So if the digits sum to <imath>9</imath>, then <imath>2A+3B</imath> is a multiple of 9. We can try plugging in numbers from our list earlier into the equation <imath>2A+3B</imath> to find what values set the expression equal to a multiple of <imath>9</imath>. By trying numbers <imath>A=6</imath>, and <imath>B=5</imath>. So then <imath>A+B</imath> yields 

<imath>6+5=\boxed{\textbf{(C)}~11}</imath>.

~NumberNinja1234
